idiom_name: Squeryl entity (KeyedEntity) + table object with insert/update in a transaction
implementation_notes: Scala's Active Record realizations come from the ORM-DSL side: with Squeryl a class extends KeyedEntity (the primary key is declared in the class), the Schema object binds it to a table (table[Book]("books")), and insert/update/delete are library statements executed inside a transaction block, so the object carries its data and the persistence calls stay typed and compiler-checked. What replaces the classic structure is the table object plus Squeryl's typed statements instead of a generated mapper; the scala-activerecord project recreates Rails' behaviour more literally, while Slick is the deliberate opposite - a functional-relational mapper with no entity objects - and is the usual choice when the team prefers data mapping.
pitfalls: Squeryl requires the persisted fields to be vars and the same instance to be used in the transaction; a case class of immutable fields cannot be updated in place.
Every statement needs a session - forgetting the transaction { } wrapper fails at runtime, not at compile time.
Typed statements only protect the columns you wrote; raw SQL or schema drift still escapes the compiler, so migrations remain a separate concern.
